title: Herd-immunity fleet broadcast of row-hammer attack signatures
idea: When any server's memory controller fires a row-hammer mitigation, it extracts a compact 'antigen' (hashed bank/row-delta/ACT-interval fingerprint) and gossips it fleet-wide within seconds; every other controller pre-loads a matching detector before the attacker reaches it, so the fleet gets vaccinated instead of each chip being infected and learning alone.
why: Row hammer (~1k-activation flips): each die can ship lighter in-DRAM mitigation (fewer tracker entries) because novel patterns are learned once and immunized everywhere; target 5-10x less mitigation area and victim-refresh overhead than per-chip worst-case provisioning.

title: Uracil-glycosylase coding: make every charge-leak an illegal symbol
idea: DNA spots cytosine deamination because uracil does not belong in DNA; since DRAM retention errors are unidirectional (true-cells leak 1->0, anti-cells 0->1), store words in constant-weight/Berger-style codes polarized per cell orientation so every leak lowers the weight, becomes an illegal codeword, and is located by direction and fixed with a cheap asymmetric (Z-channel) decoder.
why: Retention tail (<=13 fA leakers) and refresh (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% idle power): asymmetric codes correct leak errors with roughly half the check bits of symmetric BCH at equal strength, enabling ~4-8x longer refresh intervals.

title: Lesion-wiring: fine-tune each model on its own DIMM's fault map
idea: Like a developing brain rewiring around a lesion, an accelerator profiles its own HBM's weak-cell map at a relaxed 1 s refresh, then runs a short fine-tune in which exactly those weight bits are clamped to their decayed values, so the deployed model stops depending on them and weight regions run permanently at the relaxed refresh.
why: Refresh bandwidth/energy (10-20% bandwidth at 32-64 Gb) and retention tail: weights are most of inference HBM capacity; ~16x longer refresh there with <0.1% accuracy loss frees bandwidth and idle power.

title: Leaky integrate-and-fire capacitor as per-row hammer sentinel
idea: Give each small row group an analog 'membrane' capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet per ACT and leaks with a time constant matched to the refresh window; when it crosses a comparator threshold it fires a targeted neighbour refresh and resets, replacing SRAM counter tables with one array-device capacitor plus comparator per group.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations: digital per-row counters cost ~1-4% die area and grow as thresholds fall; an LIF integrator gives continuously decaying counts that cannot be gamed by window resets, at ~10x less area.

title: Physarum tube-thickening: refresh flux follows observed error flow
idea: Slime mould thickens tubes that carry flow and lets idle ones wither; each subarray holds a refresh 'conductance' that increments whenever on-die ECC corrects an error there and decays geometrically otherwise, and the refresh scheduler splits its budget in proportion, so refresh converges onto where leakage actually lives.
why: Refresh overhead: most rows retain for seconds; concentrating the budget on the ~0.1% weak regions and tracking VRT/temperature drift automatically cuts refresh energy ~5-10x.

title: Cicada prime-period sampling so hammer patterns cannot phase-lock
idea: Periodical cicadas emerge on 13- or 17-year cycles so predators cannot synchronize; run TRR sampling windows and victim-refresh slots on mutually prime, per-bank randomly reseeded periods (13/17/19/23 tREFI), so many-sided and half-double patterns that exploit fixed sampler cadence never phase-lock with all banks.
why: Row hammer: TRRespass-style bypasses exploit periodic samplers; prime-period scheduling restores probabilistic guarantees using only small LFSR state, avoiding the 2-5% area of growing trackers.

title: Kinetic-proofreading sense amp that flags marginal bits as erasures
idea: Hopfield's kinetic proofreading gains accuracy by adding a dissipative delay step; add a second timed sensing stage in which the bitline differential must survive a controlled bleed, marking cells whose signal collapses as 'erasures' rather than guesses, so the ECC decoder (which fixes two erasures for the cost of one error) repairs them.
why: Capacitor charge wall (Cs ~5 fF at AR 60-75:1): roughly doubling effective correction lets designs accept ~30-40% less cell signal, i.e. shorter, cheaper capacitors at equal failure rate.

title: Magnetosome chains: exchange-couple low-stability bits for collective retention
idea: Magnetotactic bacteria align magnetite crystals too small to be stable alone into a stable chain dipole; build fast spin cells with thermal stability ~20 kT arranged in short exchange-coupled chains whose collective stability is ~60 kT, writing by flipping one end and letting a domain wall propagate along the chain.
why: Refresh and retention tail: decouples write energy (single-cell barrier) from retention (chain barrier), ~3x lower write current than standard STT at equal retention, with no refresh and unlimited-class endurance.

title: Canary quorum: deliberately weak sentinel rows set the refresh rate
idea: Like canaries in a mine combined with bacterial quorum sensing, each bank carries a few rows built with ~30% smaller capacitance; the controller lengthens the refresh interval until a quorum of canaries across the die begins to flip and then backs off, so the main array always runs at the largest safe interval for its real temperature and age.
why: Refresh is set by worst-case datasheet margin (64 ms at 85 C); live canary feedback could run typical parts at 4-8x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss proportionally.

title: Apoptotic cascade: retire a failing page's predicted spatial accomplices
idea: Apoptotic cells signal their neighbours; when the OS retires a page for a hard error, a learned fault-cluster model of the die (shared wordline, bitline, sub-wordline driver, TSV column) pre-emptively migrates and retires the physically co-located pages most likely to fail next, before they produce uncorrectable errors.
why: Field reliability of weaker, cheaper bins: most uncorrectable errors come from spatially clustered faults; pre-emptive retirement could cut UE rates ~5-10x for <0.1% capacity, letting marginal dies ship.

title: Codon-degeneracy encoding: likely bit-flips map to near-identical values
idea: The genetic code is arranged so most point mutations yield the same or a similar amino acid; encode AI weights and activations in a learned number format whose least-significant code bits are placed in each row's measured weakest cell positions and whose code assignment is Gray-like, so the most probable flips cause the smallest numerical change.
why: ECC and refresh cost for tolerant data (most AI memory): such regions can drop the 12.5% ECC overhead and run ~10x longer refresh with negligible accuracy loss.

title: Telomerase anneal: on-die microheaters periodically reset leakage traps
idea: Embed polysilicon micro-heaters under each mat; in maintenance windows the mat's data is moved out and the mat is flash-annealed (~300 C for ~10 ms) to re-passivate the hydrogen-related interface traps and GIDL defects that create variable-retention and hammer-damaged cells, resetting the 'telomere' of the array.
why: Retention tail and aging (VRT cells force worst-case refresh): in-field healing could double to quadruple the refresh interval and extend part lifetime, letting weaker initial bins qualify.

title: Clotting capsules: liquid-metal microcapsules self-heal cracked HBM bonds
idea: Seed the HBM underfill and bond interface with ~2 um gallium-alloy microcapsules; when thermal cycling cracks a microbump or hybrid-bond pad, the crack ruptures nearby capsules and the liquid metal wicks into the gap and re-closes the circuit like a platelet plug.
why: HBM TSV tax (yield down 20-30%, field opens): converts a share of stacking and cycling opens into self-repairs, raising stack yield and life and tolerating cheaper, less tightly controlled bonding.

title: Homeostatic plasticity: sense reference self-trims to keep 50% ones
idea: Neurons scale their synapses to hold average firing constant; because bus data is scrambled, each mat's reads should average ~50% ones, so a per-mat counter tracks the running ones-fraction and nudges the sense reference/precharge level to restore balance, cancelling temperature, aging and leakage drift before it becomes errors.
why: Voltage floor (VARY ~1 V) and retention tail: recovers ~10-20% of signal margin otherwise spent as guard-band, enabling lower array voltage or smaller Cs.

title: Retinal lateral inhibition between sense amps cancels coupling noise
idea: Retinal neurons subtract a fraction of their neighbours' signals to sharpen edges; add weak, calibrated cross-coupling between adjacent bitline sense amplifiers that subtracts a set fraction of each neighbour's developing signal, cancelling the bitline-to-bitline capacitive coupling that grows at every pitch shrink.
why: Capacitor wall and pattern-dependent errors: coupling eats ~10-20% of sense signal at 12 nm-class pitch; cancelling it lets Cs shrink or bitlines lengthen (fewer sense amps, less of the 49% periphery).

title: Xylem pit valves: self-isolating subarrays contain shorts and defects
idea: Xylem pit membranes seal an embolized conduit so water reroutes; give each subarray a small isolation switch and current monitor on its local wordline supply and precharge rail, so a wordline-bitline short or gross leaker trips and seals that subarray (remapped to a spare) instead of collapsing the whole bank's voltage.
why: Yield and capital: shorts that poison entire banks are a major yield killer at aggressive pitch; containment turns bank kills into ~0.1% capacity loss, raising yield several points per wafer.

title: Thymic negative selection: random detectors that never match normal traffic
idea: The thymus deletes T-cells that react to self; at boot the controller generates thousands of random detector templates over (bank, row-delta, ACT-interval) features, deletes any that match the profiled benign workload, and keeps survivors in a tiny CAM, so traffic that triggers a survivor is flagged as non-self and throttled.
why: Row hammer: catches novel patterns (half-double, many-sided) without per-row counters, ~10x less SRAM than counter trackers with tunable false-positive rate.

title: Deinococcus polyploidy: scattered multi-copy for the critical 1% only
idea: Deinococcus radiodurans survives shattered chromosomes by keeping 4-10 genome copies and reassembling; replicate only page tables, kernel and allocator metadata 3-4x across banks with different physical neighbours and TSV columns, repairing by consensus on read, so the other 99% of memory runs with much lighter ECC.
why: ECC overhead and crash rate: crashes come mostly from corrupted metadata; strong protection of 1% lets bulk data drop from ~12.5% to ~3% check overhead.

title: Tardigrade tun state: idle pages dehydrate into strong code, slow refresh
idea: Tardigrades survive by shutting down into a protective tun; pages untouched for N seconds are compressed and rewritten with a heavy BCH/LDPC code in the space freed, and their rows move to a 10-30x slower refresh tier, rehydrating on first access.
why: Refresh at 32-64 Gb (16-33% of idle power): most memory is idle at any instant; strong coding absorbs the higher raw BER of seconds-long refresh, cutting idle refresh energy ~10x.

title: Evaporating pheromone memory: never refresh data born to expire
idea: Ant pheromone trails are useful because they evaporate; an allocator API lets software tag buffers (activations, KV-cache spills, packets, shuffle data) with a time-to-live shorter than the region's measured retention, and the controller never refreshes those rows, simply reclaiming them at expiry.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth: transient buffers are a large share of AI traffic and live microseconds to milliseconds; zero refresh for them saves their share of 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth.

title: Wolff's-law remodeling: hot rows migrate into guard-flanked bunkers
idea: Bone reinforces where it is loaded; keep a small pool of 'bunker' rows in each bank that are physically flanked by unused guard rows, and when a row's activation rate crosses a threshold the controller swaps it into a bunker, where hammering has no victims.
why: Row hammer: guarantees zero victims for the hottest rows at ~1-2% capacity cost instead of victim-refresh overhead that explodes as thresholds approach 1k.

title: Glial potassium buffering: buried sink lines soak up hammer electrons
idea: Astrocytes mop up excess K+ so neighbouring neurons do not fire spuriously; add a buried, positively biased n+ 'glial' collector line in the isolation between adjacent access transistors that captures electrons emitted by the aggressor wordline's trap-assisted charge pumping before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations: a physical root-cause fix; raising the threshold even 10x removes most tracker and victim-refresh overhead.

title: Cochlear amplifier: Hopf-poised sense amp hears sub-femtofarad cells
idea: Cochlear hair cells sit at a Hopf bifurcation, giving huge gain for faint sounds; bias each sense amplifier at the edge of oscillation with a calibrated negative-resistance loop so the tiny bitline perturbation of a ~1 fF cell tips it decisively, with per-amp calibration of the bifurcation point.
why: Capacitor charge wall: if 1-2 fF cells become readable, pillar AR can fall from 60-75:1 to ~15-20:1, cutting deposition/etch cost and opening lateral 3D capacitors.

title: Retinal filling-in: panel-scale nanoimprinted memory tolerating dead pixels
idea: Nanoimprint 2T oxide-semiconductor gain cells at F~100 nm onto Gen-10.5 display glass (~9 m2 per sheet); like the brain filling in the blind spot and dead photoreceptors, a power-up scan builds a defect map and a long Reed-Solomon erasure code reconstructs dead cells, so 1-3% dead pixels from imprint particles are acceptable.
why: Cost per GB/capital: display TFT area costs ~$50-150/m2 vs ~$100k/m2 for DRAM wafers; ~2 TB/m2 per layer gives ~$0.05/GB, ~100x below 2026 DRAM, trading latency (~100-300 ns) and areal density.

title: Exonuclease excision: per-row skip masks for 5%-defective cheap cells
idea: DNA polymerase proofreads each base and excises misincorporations; every write is read back, cells that fail are 'excised' by setting a bit in a short per-row skip mask kept in the row header, and the row's data is shifted past them on all later accesses, so a random point defect costs one cell, not a row or column.
why: Makes ultra-cheap high-defect processes (solution-processed oxide tiers, relaxed cleanroom, no laser repair) with 1-5% random dead cells usable at ~6-8% overhead, a prerequisite for ~100x cheaper media.

title: V(D)J clonal selection: wire random nanowire meshes, then select working cells
idea: The immune system generates random receptors and keeps the ones that work; spray self-assembled nanowire/nanotube networks over a coarse CMOS grid with no fine lithography, probe at test time which random junctions behave as good storage cells, and record their addresses in an on-chip translation table, discarding the rest.
why: Capital/EUV: eliminates fine patterning of the array (5-7 EUV layers, ~55% depreciation share); even at 30% junction yield plus table overhead, cost per GB could fall ~100x because the array costs almost nothing to form.

title: Population-coded bits: sixteen unreliable nanoparticle cells vote by current
idea: Synapses release vesicles with 10-90% probability yet neural populations are reliable; store each bit in ~16 spin-coated nanoparticle charge-trap sites under one coarse crosspoint, written together and read as summed current against a threshold, so up to ~5 dead or leaky sites never flip the bit.
why: Cost per GB: sites need no individual patterning, only relaxed-litho crosspoints, replacing precise devices with statistics; claimed ~100x cheaper per bit at ~3-5x latency.

title: Detritivore economy: reclaim rejected and partial-good DRAM dies
idea: Decomposers turn waste into food; buy the 10-25% of DRAM dies and HBM stacks that fail bin (retention, speed, partial array) at near-scrap prices, package them on CXL expanders whose controller maps around dead regions and runs them at 4x refresh and relaxed timing, and sell them as capacity-tier memory.
why: Supply and cost: fab yield loss is a large pool of nearly free bits; marginal cost ~1/100 of good parts, adding a few % of global bit supply with zero new fab capex.

title: Hermit-crab reuse mandate: thymus-screened retired DIMMs into CXL pools
idea: Hermit crabs live in shells others discard; a federal right-to-reuse rule plus procurement credit routes hyperscalers' decommissioned DDR4/DDR5 into CXL memory pools instead of shredders, after an automated 'thymic' stage that stress-tests each DIMM and maps out weak rows before reissue.
why: U.S. supply and cost per GB: retired server DRAM is sunk-cost capacity; reuse costs test plus CXL controller (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~50-100x below new 2026 contract DRAM.

title: Heterochromatin silencing: ship dies with no repair, OS silences bad regions
idea: Cells silence unusable genome stretches as heterochromatin instead of repairing them; design ultra-cheap-process dies with zero spare rows/columns, no fuse banks and no repair test step, store a boot-time silence map, and let the OS never allocate silenced regions, selling each die by its actual capacity.
why: Repair test time and redundancy scale with defect density and would kill a ~100x-cheaper high-defect process; removing them (plus ~3-5% spare area and fuse periphery) keeps such processes economic.

title: Coral colony tiers: build 120 monolithic tiers, keep the best 100
idea: A coral colony thrives though individual polyps die; deposit ~120 monolithic oxide-semiconductor memory tiers by low-temperature ALD/sputter with shared vertical wordline contacts, test each tier after deposition, and permanently bypass dead tiers with tier-select transistors, so ~85% tier yield still yields a full stack.
why: 3D DRAM needs 26+ tiers to break even; at ~100 EUV-free tiers cost per GB falls ~30-100x, and tier sparing removes the compound-yield wall (0.99^100) that kills deep stacks.

title: Hippocampal CA3 attractors: noisy printed crossbars that self-correct on recall
idea: CA3 recurrent networks recall whole memories from noisy cues; store data as attractors of a dense associative (modern Hopfield) network whose weights sit in a printed resistive crossbar with +-30% variation and dead devices, so iterating recall pulls errors back to the stored pattern and the array itself acts as the decoder.
why: Cost per GB: tolerates device variation that makes conventional cells useless, admitting printed/roll-to-roll media at a tiny fraction of wafer cost; trades multi-iteration latency (~us) and 3-10x capacity overhead.

title: Unihemispheric sleep: half the array maintains while the other serves
idea: Dolphins and birds sleep one brain hemisphere at a time; split ultra-leaky, ultra-cheap arrays (retention ~1 ms) into twin hemispheres that alternate, one serving reads and writes while the other runs back-to-back refresh and scrubbing, with hot lines mirrored so service never stalls.
why: Admits capacitorless or tiny-capacitor cells with 50-100x worse retention (dropping the costliest high-AR capacitor module) by accepting ~50% maintenance duty and 2x mirroring of hot lines; a ~100x path when built on stacked cheap tiers.

title: Muller's-ratchet recombination: two error-riddled copies make one clean page
idea: Sexual recombination breaks Muller's ratchet by mixing genomes with different mutations; store each page twice in very cheap cells with only an 8-bit CRC per 8-byte chunk (detect, not correct), assemble reads chunk by chunk from whichever copy passes, rewrite the failing chunk, and fall back to a rare third copy on double hits.
why: Cost per GB: replaces correction logic with detection plus duplication, so media at raw BER ~1e-5 (a 100x-cheaper class) works at ~2.25x bit overhead with trivially cheap decode.

title: Paddlefish stochastic resonance: dithered multi-reads of non-destructive cheap cells
idea: Paddlefish electroreceptors use ambient noise to detect sub-threshold prey fields; for non-destructive-read cheap gain cells whose signal sits near the sense threshold, inject a known dither on the reference and take 8-16 rapid comparator samples, averaging to resolve signals ~5x below single-shot noise.
why: Lets the cheapest cells (tiny storage nodes, mature-node or printed transistors with wide Vt spread) be read reliably by spending ~8x read latency; enabler for ~100x cheaper stacked cheap tiers.

title: Two-stage synaptic consolidation in NAND-fab charge-trap strings
idea: Synapses hold new memories in fast, fragile early-LTP and consolidate stable ones into protein-synthesis late-LTP; build DRAM-class memory on 3D-NAND-style vertical strings with ultrathin tunnel oxide (us writes, seconds retention, refreshed), and in the background 'consolidate' cold pages with a stronger pulse into deep traps that hold for hours, switching their refresh off.
why: Cost per GB: NAND-style fabs make bits at ~$0.03-0.08/GB vs ~$5-10/GB DRAM (~100x); consolidation tames refresh and wear by applying high-stress writes only to cold data.

title: Wood-frog torpor: capacitorless vertical cells run cold to stretch retention
idea: Wood frogs survive freezing by slowing their chemistry; build capacitorless floating-body cells in a 3D-NAND-like vertical channel stack and run the memory in a sealed -40 C enclosure, where junction and GIDL leakage drop ~100-1000x so millisecond room-temperature retention becomes seconds.
why: Removes the capacitor (the costliest, highest-AR module) and borrows NAND-style stacking; trades cooling energy and enclosure cost for a target ~100x lower cost per GB at rack level.

title: Honeycomb self-ordering: anodized-alumina pores as litho-free capacitor arrays
idea: Bee combs self-organize into hexagons; anodize aluminium films so pores self-order into hexagonal arrays with aspect ratio >100:1 and no lithography, use them as capacitor templates over cheap stacked access tiers, and handle domain boundaries and missing pores with a per-mat grain-boundary map that drops irregular cells from the address space.
why: Capacitor wall (AR ~115 needed) and EUV/etch cost: an electrochemical bath replaces high-AR etch and patterning; with boundary mapping as the yield fix, a key piece of a ~100x cheaper litho-free cell.

title: Phyllotaxis golden-angle interleaving so dirty-fab particle clusters scatter
idea: Plants place leaves at the golden angle so no two shade each other; map the symbols of every codeword onto cell positions along a 2D golden-ratio stride so any clustered defect (particle, scratch, leaker cluster) hits at most one symbol per codeword, letting arrays be built in a far dirtier, cheaper cleanroom with older tools.
why: Capital intensity: cleanroom class and tool cleanliness are major capex/opex; turning clustered defects into scattered singles that a modest code fixes is one lever of a ~100x cost cut on cheap substrates.

title: Murmuration checks: each cell group verifies seven neighbours in-array
idea: Starlings stay coherent by each tracking ~7 neighbours; place tiny check nodes in the CMOS under the array so each 8-cell group carries local parity shared with 7 overlapping neighbour groups (a spatially coupled LDPC evaluated locally), and the array iteratively corrects itself during refresh without shipping data to the controller.
why: Admits raw BER ~1e-3 media (orders of magnitude cheaper cells) at ~25% check overhead while keeping decode energy local; ~100x cheaper when paired with cheap-cell substrates.

title: Capsid proofreading: reversible self-assembly anneals out patterning defects
idea: Virus capsids assemble from weakly bonded subunits that unbind and rebind, so misassembled pieces fall off; pattern cell arrays with block-copolymer or DNA-tile self-assembly using cyclic annealing at temperatures where misplaced domains dissolve and correct ones persist, driving defect density to memory grade without EUV.
why: EUV capital (5-7 layers, ~55% depreciation): self-assembled 10-15 nm patterns at near-zero tool cost, with the classic DSA defect blocker fixed by thermodynamic proofreading; key route to ~100x cheaper patterning per bit.

title: Hydra conveyor: charge shifts continuously up vertical CCD strings
idea: Hydra tissue flows endlessly from body column to tentacles and is shed; use a 3D-NAND vertical string as a charge-coupled shift register, stepping charge packets along 200+ gate layers and regenerating them at a sense amp at the top of each loop, so no packet sits long enough to leak and transfer errors are reset at every regeneration.
why: Cost per GB: NAND-fab cost structure (~100x cheaper per bit), no capacitor, refresh replaced by circulation itself; trade is serial access (~us to first byte), fit for capacity tiers and streaming.

title: Chemotactic co-aged references: multilevel cheap cells read against twins
idea: E. coli chemotaxis compares the present with a methylation-held memory of a moment ago rather than absolute levels; each row of 2-3-bit-per-cell cheap storage includes reference cells written at the same instant to each level, which leak and drift alongside the data, so sensing compares data to co-aged references and drift cancels.
why: Multiplies bits per cheap cell 2-3x where leak and drift normally forbid multilevel storage; a multiplier toward ~100x with stacked cheap tiers.

title: Grid-cell residue codes: each modulus lives on a separate cheap die
idea: Entorhinal grid cells encode position with several periodic modules, a residue number system with built-in error correction; store integers and weights as residues modulo coprime moduli plus two redundant moduli, each residue on a different ultra-cheap low-yield die, so one or two dead dies are corrected and add/multiply run per residue near memory.
why: Lets 70-80% die yields and high raw error rates pass at system level with no known-good-die sort or repair, plus carry-free near-memory compute; a pathway to ~100x cheaper per GB.

title: Mycorrhizal parity pool: zero-ECC cheap modules share a common fungus
idea: Trees share nutrients through mycorrhizal networks; strip ECC chips and per-module repair from ultra-cheap memory modules and keep one shared erasure-parity pool on a CXL switch protecting hundreds of modules, rebuilding any module's failed lines on demand.
why: Amortizes protection (12.5-25% per module down to ~2-5% pool-wide) and tolerates high module failure rates, so the cheapest media classes become deployable; contributes to ~100x effective cost per GB.

title: Endosymbiotic transfer: array dies keep no brains; logic die holds all
idea: Mitochondria moved most of their genes to the nucleus; strip memory dies to bare arrays with minimal drivers (no ECC, refresh logic, repair fuses or BIST) and hybrid-bond many of them to one logic-node 'nucleus' die that does sensing, strong LDPC decoding, refresh scheduling and fault mapping for all, so arrays use the cheapest array-only process.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die; moving it to a shared logic die and letting a strong decoder accept raw-BER-1e-3 arrays roughly doubles bit density and slashes process steps; with cheap array processes it targets ~100x.
